analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics from forcing nurses to work beyond set hour limits.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to limit mandatory overtime for nurses gathered 100 cosponsors but never got a committee vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended Medicare rules so that hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers could not require a nurse to work beyond her scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a day, or more than 80 hours in two weeks. It carved out an exception for officially declared emergencies, and it gave nurses the right to report violations to the Health and Human Services Department without being fired or disciplined. Providers that knowingly violated the limits could face fines of up to $10,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses — registered nurses and licensed practical nurses — who would no longer face discipline or firing for refusing forced overtime, and hospital patients, who the bill's findings say are put at risk when exhausted nurses provide care. The bill cites research linking fatigue to medical errors and notes roughly 500,000 licensed nurses had left practice, with overtime and job dissatisfaction among the causes.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits providers from requiring a nurse to work beyond her scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in a consecutive 14-day period, except during a declared emergency.

Makes it illegal for a provider to penalize, discriminate against, or retaliate against a nurse who refuses mandatory overtime or reports a violation, including reporting the nurse to a state licensing board for refusing.

Lets nurses file complaints with the HHS Secretary, requires investigation, allows civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation, and requires public posting of penalized providers' names online.
The bill's findings cite a Harvard School of Public Health study linking staffing levels to patient outcomes and a Comptroller General report on overtime driving nurses out of the profession.
Explicitly preserves a nurse's right to voluntarily work extra hours, so the bill restricts only forced overtime.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, and clinics that participate in Medicare, which would lose mandatory overtime as a staffing tool and would need to hire more nurses or adjust schedules instead. Those added staffing costs could put pressure on Medicare payment rates.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals facing genuine nursing shortages could not fall back on forced overtime outside a declared emergency, so they might need to hire more staff, divert patients, or reduce services at a real cost.
The limits apply only to forced overtime — a nurse could still voluntarily work very long hours — so fatigue-related risk would not disappear where nurses feel economic pressure to volunteer.

Enforcement is complaint-driven: it depends on nurses coming forward to the Secretary, and the penalty for a first knowing violation is capped at $10,000, which critics could call modest for a hospital.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered patient-safety and nurse-retention benefits backed by the research it cites, at the cost of removing a flexible staffing tool from hospitals during a documented nursing shortage. The emergency exception and the voluntary-overtime carve-out address the strongest objection — that hospitals need flexibility in a crisis — though the added hiring burden during a shortage was a real cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and it never moved again before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on November 6, 2001, joined by 27 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republican Rep. Steven LaTourette.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee.
On November 14, 2001, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed.
The bill drew 100 cosponsors in total — 93 House Democrats, 6 House Republicans, and the chamber's one Independent — but no committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor.
No vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers that use mandatory overtime as a staffing method kept the practice unchanged; nurses and patients gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that rely on mandatory overtime

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as principal sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Steven LaTourette
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original Republican cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to its Health subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by sequential referral and never took it up.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic — 93 of 208 Democrats versus 6 of 223 Republicans — with a handful of Republican cosponsors and the chamber's one Independent, and no recorded floor opposition because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Hospitals would lose mandatory overtime as a way to cover shifts without hiring, and would face fines and public naming for violations. Their interest in keeping the practice runs against patient safety and nurse working conditions, which the bill's own findings say suffer under fatigue.

industries.industry: Home health agencies, clinics, and surgical centers
industries.note: These Medicare providers are also covered by the overtime limits and complaint process, so they too would have to staff within the hour caps.
